source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Ablation on failure-derived memory. On WebArena-Shopping with Gemini-2.5-flash, ReasoningBank built from successes only scored 46.5 and from successes plus failures 49.7. No-memory baseline was 39.0.
numbers: Success-only vs +failures: ReasoningBank 46.5 -> 49.7 (+3.2 pp); Synapse 40.6 -> 41.7; AWM 44.4 -> 42.2 (drops). No memory 39.0. One domain, one model, single ablation figure (Fig 7).
limits: No failure-only arm and no equal-count control, so it cannot say failures beat successes per lesson. Gain from failures is 3.2 pp on one subset. Failure items are written by an LLM with a contrastive prompt, not by a CDM-style probe of hard incidents. Baselines were not built to use failures.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 6: failure lessons add a little on top of success lessons when the extractor is designed for them; bolting failures onto a success-only method can hurt (AWM -2.2).

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank, judge-noise and step analysis
finding: The success/failure labels that feed failure lessons come from an LLM judge, and the judge is imperfect. Simulated judge accuracy from 100% down to 50% changed success rate only modestly.
numbers: Real judge accuracy 72.7% on WebArena-Shopping (Gemini-2.5-flash judge). Simulated accuracy curve: best at 100% (about 52.4 SR, read from figure); 70-90% stays roughly 49-52; 50% (random) about 47.6, still above no-memory 39.0. Steps on failed Shopping cases 8.7 (no memory) vs 2.1 (with memory).
limits: Values read off a figure; the text says only that judge accuracy does not significantly impact results. Random labels still beat no memory, which hints that part of the gain is not failure-specific content.
agent_relevance: Outcome labels, not expert probing, drive failure lessons today. The random-label result is a hint for gap 3: much of the lift may come from structure and format of the memory item, not its correctness.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) Large Language Model Agents Are Not Always Faithful Self-Evolvers (ICML 2026)
finding: Causal test of whether agents use experience. Four self-evolving frameworks, 13 backbones, 9 environments. Raw trajectories matter: removing or replacing them with irrelevant ones hurts a lot. Condensed lessons (the CDM-style output) often have little effect: corrupt, irrelevant or filler text scores nearly the same as the real lesson, and removing it changes little.
numbers: Interventions: Empty, Shuffle, Irrelevant, Corrupt, Filler. Condensed-only setting (ReasoningBank) also shows weak dependence. Pattern holds across open-weight and frontier models including Claude-Sonnet-4.6 and Qwen3-235B. Per-cell success rates are only in figures; text says condensed perturbations are nearly indistinguishable from baseline.
limits: Task regimes where pretrained priors already solve the task explain part of it. Tests existing frameworks' condensed summaries, not expert-quality CTA lessons. Numbers only seen as bar labels in extracted text.
agent_relevance: Direct hit on gap 3: in many agent setups lesson content is not what moves the score. Our test must include a length-matched irrelevant-lesson control, and should store concrete cases beside any distilled cue lesson.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks
finding: Expert-curated procedural skills lifted agent pass rates on 87 tasks across 18 model-harness configurations. Skills the agents wrote for themselves did not help and fell below no-skills.
numbers: No skills 33.9% -> curated 50.5% (+16.6 pp; range +4.1 to +25.7 across configs). Self-generated on three configs: Claude Code Opus 4.7 43.0 -> 34.9 (-8.1), Codex GPT-5.5 46.8 -> 35.5 (-11.3), Gemini CLI Gemini 3.1 Pro 36.0 -> 24.5 (-11.5); curated on the same configs +18.2 to +24.8 pp. An earlier version quoted 84 tasks, +16.2 pp, 7 configs.
limits: Authors say the self-generated deficit mixes content quality with discovery failures (10 of 12 audited trajectories never read the packs) and creator/solver interference. They list random-text and length-matched baselines as future work, so content vs structure is still untested here.
agent_relevance: Human-expert content beats self-authored content by about 25-33 pp in these harnesses. Supports using human or externally checked sources for lessons and argues against trusting self-made lessons by default. Partly informs gaps 5 and 6 as a caution.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench design ablations (quantity, length, model size)
finding: Lesson count and length saturate and then hurt. One skill gives +18.0 pp, 2-3 skills +19.0, 4 or more only +10.1. Compact +19.0 and standard +21.5 beat detailed +14.5 and comprehensive +0.7. A small model with skills (MiniMax M2.7, 34.9%) beat stronger no-skill baselines (32.7%, 29.7%).
numbers: Appendix F ablations as above. Domain gains in the latest version: Natural Science +28.8, Media +24.1, Cybersecurity +18.9, Software Engineering +11.6, Math/OR +9.7.
limits: Observational across tasks, not randomised per task; skills were written by contributors, not mined from interviews. Small-model benefit contradicts a strong-model-only gate but is for procedural tasks with verifiers.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: for curated lessons the saturation point is about 2-3 items per task, and long lessons collapse the effect. Gap 5: no strong-model-only threshold seen here; small models can gain.

source: Wray, Kirk, Laird (2024) Eliciting Problem Specifications via Large Language Models
finding: First LLM agent that plays the cognitive task analyst role (analyst, critic, refiner agents) to produce problem-space specifications for water-jug puzzles and variants. Feasibility only, no scoring against human analysts.
numbers: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (gpt-4-0125-preview), each condition run once, total API cost 3 USD. Mixed-unit and extra-jug variants: CTA agent spec correct and executable in Soar; one-shot CoT missed mixed units or left transfer unspecified. Refinement and critique steps credited for precision.
limits: Feasibility pilot, one run per condition, no human-analyst baseline and no reliability numbers. Does CTA on a puzzle class from a description, not an expert interview.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to an LLM CTA analyst found; shows an analyst-critic-refine loop is cheap and works on toy problems. Does not close gap 1 or 4.

source: Data Therapist authors (2025) Data Therapist: Eliciting Domain Knowledge from Subject Matter Experts Using LLMs
finding: GPT-4 interviewer that asks experts questions about datasets, compared with a human interviewer in a small paired study. Experts wrote more annotations with the LLM, but it was weaker at anticipating what lay readers would find hard.
numbers: 4 expert pairs (8 experts, 3 domains: accounting, political science, usable security), 45-minute sessions. DT users produced on average 4 more annotations per group; rated 5 percentage points less difficult. 58% (accounting) and 71% (usable security) of DT annotations matched human-interviewer ones. About 60% of questions were LLM-made.
limits: N=8, qualitative; the human interviewer was the study administrator (a baseline, not a gold standard). Not a critical-incident interview and no downstream test of the knowledge.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 1: an LLM interviewer gets about 58-71% overlap with a human on dataset knowledge but misses novice-confusion points, which is the CDM 'what would a novice miss' probe.

source: Kirsten et al. (2024) Decoding Complexity: Exploring Human-AI Concordance in Qualitative Coding
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 applied a human codebook to interview segments (47-person security and privacy interview study, German). Agreement with humans falls as the task becomes more interpretive, and inter-human agreement falls too.
numbers: Cohen kappa. Inter-human: Task A 0.97, B 0.83, C 0.63. GPT-4 (zero/one/few-shot): A 0.97/0.94/0.95, B 0.75/0.74/0.75, C 0.56/0.55/0.58. GPT-3.5: A 0.74/0.78/0.85, B 0.60/0.58/0.56, C 0.43/0.36/0.34. GPT-3.5 invented up to 47 non-codebook codes on Task B in one setting.
limits: Short workshop paper; segments pre-extracted by humans; codebook given, so this is applying codes, not building them. Not CDM probe coding.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: GPT-4 reaches the human ceiling on concrete codes and sits 0.05-0.20 kappa below it on harder ones; cue-action coding is probably between B and C in difficulty.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Agreement Is Not Quality: Blind Expert Verification of Human and LLM Qualitative Coding
finding: Five LLM systems and three trained humans coded 2,560 educator messages with a 72-item codebook. LLM-human agreement was lower than human-human, yet a blind domain expert preferred LLM and human code sets about equally.
numbers: Mean Jaccard human-LLM 0.30 vs human-human 0.52. 855 blind pairwise judgments: 51.5% human vs 48.5% LLM, p=0.537. Bradley-Terry ranked two LLMs above two of three humans.
limits: One domain (K-12 educator messages), one verifier. Preprint; peer review status not checked. A single expert verifier is a weak ground truth too.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: raw agreement understates LLM quality, so scoring an LLM CDM pass needs blind expert preference, not only overlap with one analyst.

source: Turpin, Michael, Perez, Bowman (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Chain-of-thought explanations omit the real driver of the answer. Adding a bias (answers reordered so correct is always A, or a suggested answer) changed predictions but was almost never mentioned in the explanation.
numbers: Accuracy drops up to 36.3% (GPT-3.5, zero-shot CoT, Suggested Answer bias) on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks; Answer-is-Always-A: GPT-3.5 -18.7%, Claude 1.0 -4.7%. CIs about +-1.6 to 2.4 points. On BBQ (2,592 examples) weak evidence was mentioned 100% of the time in 192 sampled explanations, yet stereotype influence went unmentioned.
limits: GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0 only; planted biases, not natural causes of an agent's choices. Explanations were produced with the answer, not after it.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: LLM self-reports do not reliably name the cue that caused the action. The Nisbett and Wilson worry transfers. A CDM sweep over agent traces should verify claimed cues by removing them.

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
finding: Intervened on the stated reasoning (early answering, adding mistakes, paraphrasing, filler tokens). Models vary a lot in how much they depend on their reasoning, and larger models are often less faithful.
numbers: On 7 of 8 tasks the 13B model changes its answer after CoT more often than the 175B model; on 6 of 8 tasks the 13B model was the most faithful. CoT boost not explained by extra tokens or phrasing.
limits: Anthropic internal models of 2023; 8 multiple-choice tasks. Faithfulness here means dependence on the CoT, not that the stated cause is the true cause.
agent_relevance: Gaps 9 and 5: stronger models may rationalise more, so a model's account of its own past action is weaker evidence for bigger models. Use counterfactual cue removal as the check.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Tested whether reasoning models verbalise hints that changed their answer. Reasoning models do better than non-reasoning ones but still mostly stay silent.
numbers: 6 hint types on MMLU and GPQA. Average faithfulness 25% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 39% (DeepSeek R1); misalignment hints 20% and 29%. 3.6x higher than Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 1.7x higher than DeepSeek V3. Reveal rate often below 20%. Outcome RL raises faithfulness then plateaus.
limits: Hints in the prompt, multiple-choice benchmarks where CoT is not needed; reasoning models of early 2025.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: even reasoning models name the true cue only 25-39% of the time when one exists. Cues from retrospective probes need a counterfactual check.

source: Edwards et al. (2021) Cognitive task analysis-based training in surgery: meta-analysis (bias and heterogeneity re-read)
finding: Re-read for small-study bias. The meta-analysis ran no funnel plot or trim-and-fill and pooled only four studies per outcome. Risk of bias overall was rated 'some concern', mostly missing protocols and selective reporting.
numbers: 12 studies (10 RCTs), only 5 in the meta-analysis. Heterogeneity I2 = 87% overall; 60% for knowledge (4 studies, SMD 1.36, 0.67-2.05); 61% for trainee technical (4 studies, SMD 2.06, 1.17-2.96). With the medical-student study included SMD 1.58 (0.31-2.85). MERSQI mean 13.6 (SD 1.35, range 11.0-15.5): 6 high and 6 moderate quality.
limits: No publication-bias test exists, so corrected effect sizes cannot be computed from this paper. With 4 studies per outcome a funnel plot would be uninformative anyway. Several included trials come from one lab.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: nobody has corrected the SMDs. Treat them as upper bounds; plan power for a much smaller effect.

source: Hoffman, Crandall, Shadbolt (1998) Use of the Critical Decision Method to Elicit Expert Knowledge
finding: Abstract only (Crossref): the paper discusses data quality, method reliability, efficiency and utility of CDM, with multiple-pass retrospection guided by probes. Full text and reliability statistics were not reachable (repository returned 403, publisher page blocked).
numbers: No numbers obtained. The abstract names reliability as a topic but gives no coefficient.
limits: Not opened beyond the abstract. Do not cite any reliability figure from this paper until the full text is read.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 remains open. Use the ICU-study kappa 0.64 and the 0.63-0.97 inter-human range in d08 as provisional targets.

source: Gap-search coverage note for gaps 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 (Bridge replication, LLM CDM sweep, saturation)
finding: No independent replication of Bridge was found; no study runs an LLM CDM sweep on an agent's own failed traces against plain-structure and no-lesson controls at equal tokens; no saturation sweep over number of interviews or cases was found for agent lessons. Closest are d03 and d04 (indirect).
numbers: 8 WebSearch calls used. arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs were rate limited (429, budget exhausted), so forward-citation lists of Bridge could not be pulled.
limits: Absence from a limited search, not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2 and 3 as direct tests stay open and are the experiment worth running.

source: ExpeL and subtask-memory ablations as summarised in search snippets (not opened)
finding: Secondhand from search snippets. ExpeL: random in-context example sampling hurt vs relevance-based selection; hand-crafted insights scored below LLM-extracted ones on HotpotQA. A 2026 software-engineering memory paper reports abstract insights 56.1 Pass@1 vs raw trajectories 53.4 vs vanilla 52.2 on SWE-bench Verified, and notes similar-looking but irrelevant memory adds noise.
numbers: HotpotQA hand-crafted 32.0 vs ExpeL 39.0; ALFWorld ExpeL 59.0, random sampling 42.5, ReAct 40.0 (snippet figures, unverified).
limits: Snippet only; not verified against the papers. Use as a pointer.
agent_relevance: Consistent with d03 that relevance of what is retrieved matters; supports selection by case fit (claim K05).
